answers: But such a peace, if it existed, would be the death of states. The particularities of states are so much more real and concrete, as they are not universal, as they are particular, as they are this or that, as they are this or that.

But this idea is very erroneous. For, as we have already seen (cf. § 262), it is the very nature of states to be at war, and if they remain at peace for any length of time they become degenerate. The only way to prevent this is by an increase of the military strength of the state; and as this requires expenditure of the revenues, a new war must soon be begun in order to recover this outlay.

But it is an utterly empty notion to speak of the world moving towards everlasting peace. States are as much individuals as human beings, and their peculiarities must be preserved. They are as much different from one another as human beings are, and the same number of states will always be required.

But, as the world has shown, the world cannot be at peace with itself. The particularity of nations can find its satisfaction only through the struggle and collision of the nations, and it is thus that they become conscious of themselves. The world is continually changing, and it is in the midst of this change that the unity of Spirit is maintained.

continuation.opening: Love is in general the consciousness of the unity of myself with another. I am not separate and isolated, but win my self-consciousness only by renouncing my independent existence, and by knowing myself as unity of myself with another and of another with me.
continuation.rest: But love is feeling, that is to say, the ethical in the form of the natural. It has no longer a place in the state, where one knows the unity as law, where, too, the content must be rational, and I must know it.
answers: The love of children for their parents is of this kind, in so far as they regard the parents as constituting their life. This kind of love is found also in marriage, in so far as the marriage relationship is at bottom based upon the unity of two individuals.

This renunciation is the essence of love, and in the state we find it in its most perfect form. For it is in the state alone that the individual will attains the highest point of self-consciousness, and knows its true object to be the
In love I lose myself, and at the same time, win myself again. The ethical life has as its element love, and that is the reason why the ethical is in the family.

In marriage there is likewise present the moment of renunciation, but not the complete renunciation that love is, but only a limited renunciation of my independence as regards the individual person, but as regards the family, I am the principal.

continuation.opening: As the substance, being an intelligent substance, particularises itself abstractly into many persons (the family is only a single person), into families or individuals, who exist independent and free, as private persons, it loses its ethical character:
continuation.rest: for these persons as such have in their consciousness and as their aim not the absolute unity, but their own petty selves and particular interests. Thus arises the system of atomistic: by which the substance is reduced to a general system of adjustments to connect self-subsisting extremes and their particular interests.
answers: for this consists in its being, like the person, the unity of universal and particular. As a universal, therefore, it becomes merely the system of the rights of the individual: and as the particular it is the sum of individuals in their abstract particularity.

for in its ethical being it is only a single person. Its ethical moment is therefore now only in the universal element of spirit, the state. In the state the family has its end, since its ethical being, as a single person, has now its moment in the state.

for this is the substance which makes its unity with itself its purpose, and is the medium of the mediation between the individuals and the universal. As the family is the medium between the individual and the ethical life, the state, on the other hand, is the medium between the individual and the universal, and the individual is in it a citizen.

the ethical moment is only the abstract moment, and its substance is the ethical will, which is at the same time universal in itself. The other side of this abstract moment is the subjective moment, freedom of the individual will, which is the other side of the ethical will; for this reason it is the subjective moment.

continuation.opening: The hollow object, which it produces, now fills it, therefore, with the feeling of emptiness. Its activity consists in yearning; it merely loses itself in becoming an unsubstantial shadowy object, and, rising above this loss and falling back on itself, finds itself merely as lost.
continuation.rest: In this transparent purity of its moments it becomes a sorrow-laden "beautiful soul," as it is called; its light dims and dies within it, and it vanishes as a shapeless vapour dissolving into thin air.
answers: The activity of the spirit is now that of yearning, for the beautiful soul, because it knows itself in its essential being, is itself absolute spirit.
It does not take the trouble to give itself the trouble to produce it; for the production is the same as the mere loss. It is therefore the beautiful soul.

This is the position in which conscience stands when it has got so far as to become aware of the unity of the individual and the universal spirit, or when it has got so far as to be aware of its own true nature.
The soul thus has before it a world of shadows, in which its own essence is a vanishing nothing, and in which, therefore, the truth of this essence is also lost, or which is the world of the untrue.

continuation.opening: If we go on to cast a look at the fate of these World-Historical persons, whose vocation it was to be the agents of the World-Spirit,—we shall find it to have been no happy one. They attained no calm enjoyment;
continuation.rest: their whole life was labour and trouble; their whole nature was nought else but their master-passion. When their object is attained they fall off like empty hulls from the kernel. They die early, like Alexander; they are murdered, like Caesar; transported to St. Helena, like Napoleon.
answers: they were often unhappy and even miserably ruined; and, even in their most successful periods, they were always men of restless spirits and intractable characters. We must not demand for them a happy, contented life, since the world's business is not conducted by such.

they were often the victims of the very necessities which they served; they were the playthings and toys of events which they themselves excited. It is not by accident that they have been the victims of their own work, for they have brought it to pass.
their lives were as tempestuous as the work which they performed. In the course of their actions, they came to know the reality of the World-Spirit, and had to carry out its work.

the very substance of their life was the fulfilment of a task, which involved the most violent collisions with the passions that prevail in the world: a task that is not of a moral character, which must not be regarded as a moral duty, and which can only be attained through the most painful struggles.

continuation.opening: Here there is a self-consciousness for a self-consciousness, at first immediately as one of two things for another. In that other as ego I behold myself, and yet also an immediately existing object, another ego absolutely independent of me and opposed to me.
continuation.rest: (The suppression of the singleness of self-consciousness was only a first step in the suppression, and it merely led to the characterisation of it as particular.) This contradiction gives either self-consciousness the impulse to show itself as a free self, and to exist as such for the other:—the process of recognition.
answers: As such the other ego is in relation to me as a thing, as the most abstract thing, an ego, that is to say an absolutely free substance, whose being-for-self is its own ego. I am for the other ego the same as the other ego is for me; each is the same for the other as a thing, as an immediately free substance.

The first movement of the spirit is thus an infinite movement; it is the same as in the relation between master and servant. The one self-consciousness is self-conscious as object and as subject; and it is for the other subject only as object, and that other is for it itself an object.

§ 430. But in this my ego there is also present the essential nature of spirit, which is self-consciousness for an other; it is a spirit, which, by virtue of the very nature of its being, is for me, and is not, therefore, merely a thing, or a thing for me, but is for me, and for itself, an ego, and in that its other.

I am a self-consciousness which is self-conscious for itself, and yet which is also an object for another. And just as much as my own self-consciousness is a self for itself, as much also is the other a self for itself.

continuation.opening: Only one word more concerning the desire to teach the world what it ought to be. For such a purpose philosophy at least always comes too late. Philosophy, as the thought of the world, does not appear until reality has completed its formative process, and made itself ready.
continuation.rest: History thus corroborates the teaching of the conception that only in the maturity of reality does the ideal appear as counterpart to the real, apprehends the real world in its substance, and shapes it into an intellectual kingdom. When philosophy paints its grey in grey, one form of life has become old, and by means of grey it cannot be rejuvenated, but only known. The owl of Minerva takes its flight only when the shades of night are gathering.
answers: The thought of the world, at this point of time, is able to comprehend itself, but it is not capable of influencing it in this sense of the word, for the truth, when it has assumed the form of thought, comes into the world too late, to be of any practical use for the course of the world.

Philosophy, as the thought of the world, appears too late to shape the world in accordance with its own ideal, for it grasps that ideal only as something that has already existed. But the thought of the world is not only in point of time later than the empirical existence of the world, but, inasmuch as it is the thought, it is also later than the world as such.

It can in this way describe the spirit of the times in its own element, and only when its work of forming is finished is it able to comprehend it in thought. Therefore the famous saying of the owl of Minerva is true, that its wisdom flies at the approach of night. When this philosophy comes, a form of the world has grown old. It is not in this philosophy that it can find its new beauty.

At that time philosophy only depicts it in the form of thought, and cannot lead it any further. The rose in the meadow is not plucked by this knowledge, the lightning is not deflected from the cloud by this knowledge, and the world is not improved by philosophy. For philosophy is the world in its maturity, the world as it has reached the end of its development.

continuation.opening: To apprehend what is is the task of philosophy, because what is is reason. As for the individual, every one is a son of his time; so philosophy also is its time apprehended in thoughts.
continuation.rest: It is just as foolish to fancy that any philosophy can transcend its present world, as that an individual could leap out of his time or jump over Rhodes. If a theory transgresses its time, and builds up a world as it ought to be, it has an existence merely in the unstable element of opinion, which gives room to every wandering fancy.
answers: As such, it does not go beyond its time or its contemporaneous world, nor, for that matter, does philosophy ever go beyond the real world to some other world beyond, for thought can find nothing outside of its time. In this respect philosophy is no more privileged than the individual; for the same reason, however, it has a different importance, for the individual may be lacking to himself, but reason, and therefore also philosophy, can lack nothing to itself.
It is impossible to get beyond this time, just as impossible to get above one's own time or above one's own epoch.

Philosophy cannot do and must not do more than to depict the time in which it lives in the shape of thought, and to know as well as to depict this. To invent an ideal world beyond the world is not philosophy's business. Philosophy is not entitled to tell the world how it ought to be.

For this reason, too, no one can demand of philosophy that it should transcend his own time. Philosophy is in the world, and not in another world; and the world is a rational world; consequently the rational world is the world of philosophy.

continuation.opening: A person must give to his freedom an external sphere, in order that he may reach the completeness implied in the idea. Since a person is as yet the first abstract phase of the completely existent, infinite will, the external sphere of freedom is not only distinguishable from him but directly different and separable.
continuation.rest: The reasonableness of property consists not in its satisfying our needs, but in its superseding and replacing the subjective phase of personality. It is in possession first of all that the person becomes rational. The first realization of my freedom in an external object is an imperfect one, it is true, but it is the only realization possible so long as the abstract personality has this first-hand relation to its object.
answers: The will is therefore capable of separating the external thing from itself, of withdrawing from it, of giving it up as its own and disposing of it; and this act is the will's act of self-affirmation and self-existence. The external thing is a thing of nature, or else the product of the will; and the distinction between these two cases is of very great importance in determining the nature and mode of ownership.

The person therefore has property, which is an external thing. Property is therefore a right of the person, and is as it were the first embodiment of the person. The first embodiment of the infinite will is not as yet the free personality, and therefore not as yet the free spirit. This is what determines the form in which the external sphere exists, and the kind of content it has.
This is the possession which is the property of a person, his own property.

The sphere is the will, which has not yet become aware of its own nature, but still exists for itself in the form of nature, which is the material of the human spirit, as of the spirit in general. The human being must appropriate this sphere for his freedom, and the first phase of appropriation is the phase of immediate appropriation, i.e. possession.

continuation.opening: The injury which the criminal experiences is inherently just because it expresses his own inherent will, is a visible proof of his freedom and is his right. But more than that, the injury is a right of the criminal himself, and is implied in his realized will or act.
continuation.rest: In his act, the act of a rational being, is involved a universal element, which by the act is set up as a law. This law he has recognized in his act, and has consented to be placed under it as under his right.
answers: The injury is a negative act in virtue of the fact that the will of the criminal is limited and conditioned by something other than the universal will which it is. This negative act has the nature of a condition or limitation.
The criminal is a free being and must therefore be recognized and treated as such. His wrong-doing, though it is not to be recognized as just or good, is yet a free act, and is his own act.
For in this his act he has done the injury, but by the very fact that it is done by him the act is not right, and is therefore an injury to himself, inasmuch as he is a right-having person.
In this injury the criminal is at the same time not wronged, but, on the contrary, is right. It follows from this that to inflict punishment on him is just.

continuation.opening: It is easy for one to grasp the notion that the state is the self-determining and completely sovereign will, whose judgment is final. It is more difficult to apprehend this "I will" as a person. By this is not meant that the monarch can be wilful in his acts.
continuation.rest: Rather is he bound to the concrete content of the advice of his councillors, and, when the constitution is established, he has often nothing to do but sign his name. But this name is weighty. It is the summit, over which nothing can climb.
answers: On the contrary, it is necessary for him to be objective in the sense that he should conform to the laws which have been formulated and adopted through his own will, and that these laws should be binding for him as for everyone else.

He is the embodiment of the state as the self-determining will; and the self-determining will has the character of being free from the content that determines it. This is the same as saying that he is the person.

For in that case his acts would be in opposition to his will as sovereign, which would be as irrational as any other. The "I will" is the will which knows what it wills, and is not bound by any other will.

His will must be in accordance with the rational will. His person is the one point in which the universal and particular aspects are united. The rational will is not merely the general will of the people or of the legislature, but the particular will of the monarch, who is in the first instance a person.

continuation.opening: The German Spirit is the Spirit of the new World. Its aim is the realization of absolute Truth as the unlimited self-determination of Freedom—that Freedom which has its own absolute form itself as its purport. The destiny of the German peoples is, to be the bearers of the Christian principle.
continuation.rest: The principle of Spiritual Freedom—of Reconciliation [of the Objective and Subjective],was introduced into the still simple, unformed minds of those peoples; and the part assigned them in the service of the World-Spirit was that of not merely possessing the Idea of Freedom as the substratum of their religious conceptions, but of producing it in free and spontaneous developments from their subjective self-consciousness.
answers: In the course of history we find that Spirit has made the effort to realize its aim by means of the State, and it is to the German peoples that has been given this task. It is only in the State that we have the rational reality of Spirit, and the end of Spirit is to know itself in this rational reality.

The Greek and the Roman Spirit was a Spirit of immediate Nature, not yet conscious of itself; the Spirit of the Oriental World was the Spirit of the One, in the form of the unlimited abstraction of the Idea. The German World is the World of Spirit, which is the Spirit of the new World.

In the Roman empire we found the world-historical nation in its highest form, in the state. In the Christian principle, however, Freedom is exalted to a higher stage. It is no longer a limited freedom of the state, but the unlimited freedom of the Spirit, as Spirit. This freedom is not the freedom of the individual, but the freedom of the Spirit.

The history of the modern world is the history of the realization of Freedom. It is divided into three principal stages, the first of which is that of the East, the second that of Greece and Rome, and the third that of Germany. In the East Freedom has its home in the One; in Greece and Rome in the Many; in Germany all have reached Freedom.
